tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

Its first sentence is the sidebar status. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). action.description:

* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

1	# D4 brief: the biology deep dive (Round 4, 14 Nov 2026, about 00:40 AM India time)
2	
3	Read this whole file, then read `D0-brief.md` sections 3 to 6 and 8 in this folder. D0's fact rule, schemas, note layout and style apply in full. Where this file adds to D0, this file wins.
4	
5	## Why this round
6	
7	The team's document is built on trial abstracts and policy papers. It has little of the physiology underneath: why one patient responds to a drug and another does not, how fast a dose change works, how much blood pressure moves on its own, why each safety check exists, which lab values matter and how fast they move, and how to tell from the body (not from the patient's word) whether the medicine was taken. That layer is what would make the product hard to copy. The reader of your note is the team's biology student, who will turn it into protocol rules and product features.
8	
9	## The product it serves
10	
11	A home blood-pressure step loop for India. A patient sends home cuff readings. Software runs the state's published step protocol (Gujarat HEARTS sheet) from a data file and drafts a dose change; a doctor approves it with one tap. Before any step-up it asks whether the medicine was taken. The protocol: step 1 amlodipine 5 mg; step 2 amlodipine 10 mg ("after 30 days measure BP again, if still high"); step 3 add telmisartan 40 mg; step 4 telmisartan 80 mg (requires blood sugar, urea, creatinine, urine protein; abnormal means refer; if no specialist, withdraw telmisartan and add chlorthalidone); step 5 add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if unavailable). Telmisartan and chlorthalidone are barred in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age without effective contraception. A Nigeria protocol uses losartan. The loop uses home readings: two readings 1 minute apart, morning and evening, on days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle; at least 3 valid days, aiming for 7; "still high" is a home mean of 135/85 or more; 180/110 or more triggers urgent review.
12	
13	These are the drugs to centre on: **amlodipine, telmisartan, chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide** (and losartan). Other classes (ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, spironolactone) matter where they explain a mechanism or a signal.
14	
15	## Source rules for this round
16	
17	- **Primary sources first:** physiology and pharmacology papers, pharmacokinetic studies, drug labels (DailyMed, FDA labels, EMA SmPCs, CDSCO where available), guideline documents (ESH 2023, ISH 2020, ACC/AHA 2017 or later, WHO 2021, NICE NG136, Indian guidelines), meta-analyses and named trials. Use Europe PMC (`https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=...&format=json&resultType=core` returns abstracts) and PubMed E-utilities (`efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=...&rettype=abstract&retmode=text`) as in D0. The Lancet and PubMed web pages often refuse the fetch tool; go through Europe PMC instead.
18	- Record each fact with **the mechanism as well as the number** where the source gives it ("telmisartan blocks the AT1 receptor, so the efferent arteriole of the glomerulus relaxes and filtration pressure falls, so creatinine rises a little" is what the biology student needs).

Potassium: high on ARBs, low on thiazides; the thresholds labels and guidelines use; why it matters for the heart. 1	# D0 brief: rules for every research agent (Beyond Next Ventures challenge, SPARK Night)
2	
3	Read this whole file before you start. Where it disagrees with any other instruction file (including the deep-research skill's `researcher.md`), this file wins.
4	
5	## 1. What this is for
6	
7	A student team (computer science + hardware + biology, Ashoka University, India) is in an overnight deep-tech buildathon RIGHT NOW: 13 Nov 2026 6 PM to 14 Nov 2026 noon, India time. By noon they must show a clearly defined problem, a working prototype, first test results and a one-page "Deep Tech Thesis". Kits hold common maker parts (ESP32 or Arduino boards, breadboards, basic sensors). Anything specialist must be borrowed, bought locally tonight, or replaced by a phone.
8	
9	The challenge, set by the venture fund Beyond Next Ventures (verbatim):
10	
11	> We need ways to manage chronic disease burden at scale despite limited access to resources, specialists and irregular clinical follow-ups. Patients need treatment methods that responds to their specific condition, and will remain adaptive to patient needs between appointments. How can digital therapeutics use rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers to continuously personalise care, thereby bringing measurable improvements in health outcomes to patients who cannot access frequent specialist support? The opportunity is to extend effective treatment into everyday life, beyond monitoring and reminders.
12	
13	A coordinator combines your note with others into one long document. You gather and record facts. You do not rank options and you do not write conclusions.
14	
15	## 2. Scope defaults
16	
17	- India first. Then global evidence. Japan matters because it is the fund's home.
18	- "Digital therapeutic" here means software (often with a device) that changes the treatment itself for one patient: the dose, the next step of a protocol, the exercise, the diet plan, the stimulation. Dashboards and reminders alone do not count, but record the evidence about them, because the challenge says "beyond monitoring and reminders".
19	- "Adaptive depth" scale, used for every product and programme: 0 = uses no patient data; 1 = shows data (monitoring); 2 = reminders and generic content; 3 = personalised coaching from the person's own data; 4 = changes the therapy itself by protocol or algorithm (dose, protocol step, exercise prescription), with or without a clinician signing off.
20	- State of play as of November 2026. The coordinator's own knowledge stops in mid-2026 and may be stale, so check for 2026 events.
21	
22	## 3. Speed and saving
23	
24	- Time box: about 20 minutes. Stop at your search allowance (it is in your task).
25	- FIRST create your note file with its title and an empty Digest. Then append findings after every 5 to 8 searches. An agent that stalls must leave its work on disk.
26	- Cover the highest-value questions first.
27	- Not searched: write `NOT SEARCHED: <what>`. Looked for and not found: write `NOT FOUND: <what>`. Never guess.
28	- Prefer direct fetches of known sources, which need no search:
29	  - PubMed: `https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=...` or `https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=json&term=...` then `esummary.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=json&id=...`
30	  - Europe PMC: `https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=...&format=json`
31	  - ClinicalTrials.gov: `https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=...`
32	  - openFDA devices: `https://api.fda.gov/device/510k.json?search=...`
33	  - arXiv: `http://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=...`
34	  - regulator pages, company pages, journal pages, GitHub.
35	- Blocked or limited: reddit.com (use the Arctic Shift API sparingly), LinkedIn, X and Instagram (search snippets only; never reconstruct a post you could not read).
36	- End the note with `Searches used: N`.
37	
38	## 4. The fact rule (the most important rule)
39	
40	- Every fact is one bullet or table row with: an ID (`<note code>-F<number>`, for example `D1-03-F12`), the value with its unit, the year the value refers to, the source URL, the date of the source item (or "undated"), and OPENED (you opened the page and saw the value) or SNIPPET (search snippet only).
41	- Open the primary source for every number that matters. A SNIPPET number is second class and must be labelled.
42	- Quotes: 25 words or fewer, verbatim, only from a page you opened.
43	- Your own memory is a lead, never a source. The leads in your task are also only leads: confirm each one or mark it NOT FOUND.
44	- Figures that conflict: record both, with dates and sources. Do not pick one.
45	- Tag each fact: CITED (published figure, source opened), THEIR CLAIM (a company says it about itself), OUR ARITHMETIC (you computed it; show the sum), SOURCE ESTIMATE (the source itself estimates or models), SNIPPET.
46	- Time-sensitive facts (prices, laws, funding, whether a company is alive) carry their date.
47	
48	## 5. Schemas
49	
50	**A study.** Name and year; design (randomised trial, cluster trial, cohort, review); size; country and setting; who was compared with whom; primary outcome; effect with its confidence interval or p value; length of follow-up; funder; main limits; URL. Record null and negative results as carefully as positive ones. Flag India and other low-resource evidence.
51	
52	**A company, product or programme.** What it is in one line; country; what it measures (device or biomarker); what it changes in the therapy; adaptive depth 0-4; who is in the loop (doctor, nurse, coach, nobody); evidence (trial? peer-reviewed? own data only?); regulatory status; price to the patient or payer; funding (amount, date, lead investor, or participant only); traction (THEIR CLAIM, with date); status as of Nov 2026 (alive, acquired, pivoted, shut); URL.
53	
54	**A person.** Two independent sources tying the person to the role. If a namesake exists, say which one you rejected and why.

58	```

61	## Digest
62	(400 words at most: the 12 facts that matter most for deciding what to build tonight, each with its fact ID; 3 surprises; anything that contradicts the starting leads in section 7.)
63	
64	## Findings
65	(grouped under the key questions in your task)
66	
67	## NOT FOUND / NOT SEARCHED
68	
69	Searches used: N
70	```

72	## 7. Starting leads to break
73	
74	The coordinator's unverified starting ideas. Look for evidence against them as hard as evidence for them.
75	
76	1. Programmes that change the treatment from home readings (dose titration, protocol steps) improve outcomes; monitoring and reminders alone mostly do not.
77	2. In India the binding limit is the prescriber's time and the gap between visits, so the workable design keeps a doctor or health worker approving each change while software does the reading, the protocol logic and the drafting.
78	3. Candidate loops: (a) home blood-pressure readings driving a stepwise medicine protocol; (b) fasting-glucose readings driving insulin dose changes in type 2 diabetes; (c) an inhaler or breathing sensor plus air-quality data adapting an asthma or COPD plan; (d) phone-camera and pulse-sensor rehabilitation that adapts each session.
79	4. The durable advantage is outcome data, clinical validation and distribution, not the app.
80	5. The honest regulatory route is decision support with clinician sign-off first; autonomous dosing needs a licence later.
81	
82	## 8. Style
83	
84	Dense, factual, plain words, short sentences. No marketing language. No em dashes. Rupees with Indian grouping (₹1,200; ₹844 crore). Give US dollar figures as published.

1	# D4-02 How fast a dose change works (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)
2	
3	## Digest
4	
5	12 facts that matter most:
6	
7	1. Steady state: amlodipine 7 to 8 days (F01); telmisartan about 4 to 5 days (F05, our arithmetic); chlorthalidone about 7 to 12 days (F08, our arithmetic); HCTZ 1 to 3 days (F11).
8	2. Across 18 trials, half of the full BP fall arrives in about 1 week, whatever the class (F36); if exponential, about 78% at 2 weeks and 95% at 4 (F37, our arithmetic).
9	3. Telmisartan: US label, most effect within 2 weeks, maximum by about 4 (F06); EU-style SmPC, maximum at 4 to 8 weeks, a caution before raising the dose (F43).
10	4. Amlodipine label: "wait 7 to 14 days between titration steps" (F03); a 1987 trial titrated every 2 weeks (F35).
11	5. Thiazides: early fall from salt and water loss, lasting fall from lower vessel resistance by 6 to 8 weeks (F39). In an Indian ambulatory trial chlorthalidone's week-4 effect was about 56% of week 12 (F44); office data show most by week 2 (F41, F10).
12	6. HCTZ 12.5 mg did not lower 24-h BP in the Indian trial; it wears off within the day (F42).
13	7. WHO 2021: monthly until target, low certainty (F18). ESH 2023: monthly, but 2-weekly visits gave earlier control (observational plus 1 small RCT); no "rigid rules" (F20). ISH: control within 3 months (F19). NICE: no interval (F22).
14	8. India: the Punjab IHCI sheet allows titration "at 15 days frequency if required" (F15); Madhya Pradesh says 30 days only (F16).
15	9. IHCI Punjab and Maharashtra: 70 to 76% controlled on amlodipine 5 mg; control plateaued at 77 to 82% from step 3 or 4 (F17).
16	10. Faster titration: 2-weekly protocol visits beat usual care at 12 months in a 156-patient RCT (F24); 2-week encounter intervals normalised BP in 0.7 vs 1.9 months (observational, F25).
17	11. Safety data on faster loops are thin: similar adverse events with monthly home-guided titration (F28); no falls or hypotension in a 42-patient pilot (F31); no stops for adverse events with accelerated titration in Nigeria (F34).
18	12. Once controlled, 6-monthly review equalled 3-monthly (F27).
19	
20	Surprises: India's Punjab sheet already permits 15-day steps (F15). US and EU telmisartan texts disagree, 4 vs 4 to 8 weeks (F06, F43). Chlorthalidone's ambulatory effect kept growing after week 4 (F44).
21	
22	Against the starting leads: the evidence that faster stepping helps is mostly observational (F25, F26), and later protocol steps added few controlled patients in IHCI (F17).
23	
24	## What this suggests for the product
25	
26	- Suggestion: keep 30 days as the default step. Readings on days 24 to 30 sit at about 93 to 96% of the expected full effect (OUR ARITHMETIC from F36: 1 - 0.5^(3.43/0.91) = 0.93; 1 - 0.5^(4.29/0.91) = 0.96).
27	- Suggestion: a 14-day step (readings days 8 to 14) would see only about 58 to 78% of the full effect (OUR ARITHMETIC, same model, F37). The loop would then step up some patients whose current dose would have worked. Offer it only where a label or an Indian sheet supports it: amlodipine 5 to 10 mg (F03, F15, F35).
28	- Suggestion: no fast track after starting or raising chlorthalidone or HCTZ (F39, F44), or telmisartan 40 to 80 mg (F43). If the reading is "still high" but close to 135/85, allow one more 30-day cycle at the same dose.
29	- Suggestion: start counting the reading window only after steady state. That is about day 8 for amlodipine and day 12 for chlorthalidone (F01, F08).
30	- Suggestion: store a predicted response curve for each step (t50 about 1 week, F36). A day-14 home mean with almost no fall should trigger the "was the medicine taken" question early, without stepping up early.
31	- Suggestion: if HCTZ replaces chlorthalidone, record the time of dose and reading. HCTZ's short action (F11, F42) can make morning pre-dose readings look high.
32	- Suggestion: once controlled, drop to sparse home checks (F27, F19).
33	- Suggestion: log side effects at every step. IHCI could not (F17), so the product's own data would be new evidence on faster stepping (F31, F34).
34	
35	## Findings
36	
37	### Q1. Half-life, steady state and time to near-full effect, drug by drug
38	
39	Labels read through the openFDA label API (full SPL text); the DailyMed URL given is the same set ID. All are US labels; no Indian (CDSCO) label text was opened.
40	
41	- D4-02-F01 | Amlodipine half-life and steady state | Terminal elimination half-life about 30 to 50 hours; steady-state plasma levels reached after 7 to 8 days of daily dosing; kinetics not much changed by kidney failure. Our gloss (OUR ARITHMETIC): a drug reaches about 94 to 97% of steady state after 4 to 5 half-lives, so a 30 to 50 h half-life gives 5 to 10 days, matching the label. Norvasc label 2023. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=7367289c-b0b0-466a-83e2-558e2985c29f | label effective 2023-02-15 | OPENED | CITED
42	- D4-02-F02 | Amlodipine slow onset mechanism | Label: amlodipine's interaction with the calcium channel "is characterized by a gradual rate of association and dissociation with the receptor binding site, resulting in a gradual onset of effect". It is a peripheral arterial vasodilator acting on vascular smooth muscle, lowering peripheral resistance. Our gloss: the effect builds over days as plasma level and receptor binding both rise. Norvasc label 2023. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=7367289c-b0b0-466a-83e2-558e2985c29f | label effective 2023-02-15 | OPENED | CITED
43	- D4-02-F03 | Amlodipine label titration interval | Label: "In general, wait 7 to 14 days between titration steps. Titrate more rapidly, however, if clinically warranted, provided the patient is assessed frequently." Usual start 5 mg, maximum 10 mg once daily. Label gives no explicit weeks-to-maximal-effect figure. Norvasc label 2023. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=7367289c-b0b0-466a-83e2-558e2985c29f | label effective 2023-02-15 | OPENED | CITED
44	- D4-02-F04 | Amlodipine trough-to-peak | 15 placebo-controlled trials (800 on amlodipine, 538 placebo): placebo-corrected fall at 24 h post-dose about 12/6 mmHg standing and 13/7 mmHg supine, "with little difference in peak and trough effect"; no tolerance up to 1 year. Our gloss: a home reading at any time of day should reflect the drug fairly evenly. Norvasc label 2023. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=7367289c-b0b0-466a-83e2-558e2985c29f | label effective 2023-02-15 | OPENED | CITED
45	- D4-02-F05 | Telmisartan half-life and accumulation | Terminal elimination half-life about 24 hours; trough plasma level 10 to 25% of peak; accumulation index 1.5 to 2.0 with once-daily dosing; nonlinear (greater than proportional) plasma levels from 20 to 160 mg; cleared almost entirely in bile, not urine; no initial dose change needed in kidney impairment. Steady state is not stated as days in the label; by the 4 to 5 half-life rule it is about 4 to 5 days (OUR ARITHMETIC: 24 h x 4 to 5 = 96 to 120 h). Telmisartan tablets label (Amneal) 2023. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=20a60231-64f0-4751-aa81-6c0e64334179 | label effective 2023-09-30 | OPENED | CITED
46	- D4-02-F06 | Telmisartan time to full effect (label) | Dosage section: "Most of the antihypertensive effect is apparent within 2 weeks and maximal reduction is generally attained after 4 weeks." Pharmacodynamics: blood pressure falls after the first dose, "with a maximal reduction by about 4 weeks"; on stopping, BP returns to baseline over several days to one week. Placebo-subtracted trough falls about 6-8/6 mmHg (20 mg), 9-13/6-8 (40 mg), 12-13/7-8 (80 mg); 160 mg gave no further fall. Telmisartan tablets label 2023. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=20a60231-64f0-4751-aa81-6c0e64334179 | label effective 2023-09-30 | OPENED | CITED
47	- D4-02-F07 | Telmisartan onset within 3 hours (Micardis HCT label) | Micardis HCT label: "The onset of antihypertensive activity occurs within 3 hours, with a maximal reduction by approximately 4 weeks." Same label: telmisartan-HCTZ dose "can be titrated up to 160 mg/25 mg after 2 to 4 weeks, if necessary." Micardis HCT label 2024. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=b078dae2-664d-4144-847a-3b9d9b557402 | label effective 2024-12-31 | OPENED | CITED
48	- D4-02-F08 | Chlorthalidone half-life | Generic chlorthalidone label: diuretic action "prolonged (48-72 hours)"; diuretic effect starts in about 2.6 hours and lasts up to 72 hours; mean half-life 40 hours after 50 to 200 mg (53 h after 50 mg, 60 h after 100 mg); about 75% protein-bound, which the label attributes to "an increased affinity of the drug to erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase" (red-cell binding is our lead for the long half-life, not a label claim). Thalitone label: mean plasma half-life about 40 to 60 hours, eliminated mainly unchanged in urine. Steady state by 4 to 5 half-lives: about 7 to 12 days (OUR ARITHMETIC: 40 to 60 h x 4 to 5 = 160 to 300 h). Chlorthalidone label (Unichem) 2022. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=01065eda-7515-46bc-b858-a062c3aa35bd | label effective 2022-11-24 | OPENED | CITED
49	- D4-02-F09 | Chlorthalidone label titration interval | Thalitone (15 mg tablet, not interchangeable with other chlorthalidone): "After 2 weeks, the dosage may be increased to a single daily dose of 25 mg if additional blood pressure reduction is needed"; doses above 25 mg not expected to lower BP more. Generic label: start 25 mg, raise to 50 mg "if the response is insufficient after a suitable trial" (no interval given); uric acid rises and potassium falls with dose over 25 to 100 mg. Thalitone label 2026. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label effective 2026-06-25 | OPENED | CITED
50	- D4-02-F10 | Chlorthalidone effect at 2 to 12 weeks (Thalitone trials) | Two 12-week placebo-controlled trials: standing systolic fall with Thalitone 15 mg averaged -11.77 vs -1.89 mmHg placebo over weeks 2 to 12, and -12.43 vs -2.02 over weeks 4 to 12, so the averaged effect from week 4 on was only slightly larger than from week 2 on. Potassium fell by week 4 (-0.35 mmol/L on 15 mg; -0.53 on 25 mg) and stayed there at week 12 (-0.31; -0.55). Uric acid up by week 4 (+0.66 mg/dL on 15 mg; +1.04 on 25 mg). Thalitone label 2026. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=bc5a0299-115b-4e60-bb3f-c75a95c51c15 | label effective 2026-06-25 | OPENED | CITED
51	- D4-02-F11 | Hydrochlorothiazide half-life and diuresis | Plasma half-life 5.6 to 14.8 hours; at least 61% excreted unchanged within 24 h; diuresis begins within 2 h, peaks about 4 h, lasts 6 to 12 h. Half-life doubles in mild-moderate and triples in severe kidney impairment (olmesartan-HCTZ label). Label: mechanism of the antihypertensive effect "is unknown"; usual start 25 mg, may rise to 50 mg; no interval given. Steady state about 1 to 3 days (OUR ARITHMETIC: 5.6 to 14.8 h x 5). HCTZ tablets label 2023. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=01ad3531-5ed9-434c-b7d5-02d72aa82e46 | label effective 2023-12-25 | OPENED | CITED
52	- D4-02-F12 | HCTZ combination: onset within 1 week, near maximal at 4 weeks | Olmesartan-HCTZ label, factorial trial: "The antihypertensive effect had onset within 1 week and was near maximal at 4 weeks." Olmesartan alone: onset within 1 week, "largely manifest after 2 weeks". Olmesartan-HCTZ label (AvKARE) 2026. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=017bc6a3-5b3d-2381-e063-6394a90abece | label effective 2026-01-19 | OPENED | CITED
53	- D4-02-F13 | Losartan half-life and time course | Losartan half-life about 2 hours; its active carboxylic acid metabolite, which the label says is "responsible for most of the angiotensin II receptor antagonism" (about 14% of a dose is converted), 6 to 9 hours. Label titration: start 50 mg, may rise to 100 mg (no interval given; in the label's RENAAL trial (type 2 diabetic nephropathy), investigators titrated to 100 mg "After one month" if trough BP was not under 140/90). Cozaar label 2026. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=9949448f-c3b9-44ee-94ed-c1aca8c90f39 | label effective 2026-01-20 | OPENED | CITED
54	- D4-02-F14 | Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor, for contrast) | Lisinopril-HCTZ label: onset 1 h, peak fall by 6 h, "In some patients achievement of optimal blood pressure reduction may require two to four weeks of therapy." Lisinopril-HCTZ label 2026. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=00b266d9-ac4a-e931-e063-6294a90a6a0b | label effective 2026-10-01 | OPENED | CITED

56	### Q2. Guideline intervals between titration steps
57	
58	- D4-02-F15 | India IHCI state sheet (Punjab): 30 days, or 15 days if required | Punjab "Hypertension Protocol" sheet (India Hypertension Management Initiative, version "Punjab 1.00-5-15"): each step reads "After 30 days# measure BP again. If still high"; the # footnote says "Dose of anti-hypertension medications can be titrated at 15 days frequency if required." Steps: amlodipine 5, 10; add telmisartan 40, 80; add chlorthalidone 12.5, 25; then check adherence and refer. HCTZ 25 mg start, 50 mg intensification if chlorthalidone unavailable. https://resolvetosavelives.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/punjab-a1-hypertension-protocol.pdf | sheet undated (uploaded 2023-09) | OPENED | CITED
59	- D4-02-F16 | India IHCI state sheet (Madhya Pradesh): 30 days, no faster option | Madhya Pradesh sheet: same six steps, "After 30 days, measure BP again" at each; no 15-day footnote. Footnote at telmisartan 80 mg: blood sugar, urea, creatinine and urine protein before raising the dose; abnormal means refer; if no specialist, withdraw telmisartan and add chlorthalidone (the same wording as the product's Gujarat protocol). https://resolvetosavelives.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/mp-a1-hypertension-protocol.pdf | sheet undated (uploaded 2023-09) | OPENED | CITED
60	- D4-02-F17 | IHCI Punjab and Maharashtra: control by step, 30-day reviews (India) | Programme records 2018 to 2021, 281,209 started on amlodipine 5 mg, 159,292 seen in Jan to Mar 2022. Reviews every 30 days. Punjab: 70% controlled (<140/90) on amlodipine 5 mg, 75% cumulative at amlodipine 10 mg, 77% after adding telmisartan 40 mg, plateau at 77% from step 4. Maharashtra (step 2 = add telmisartan 40): 76% then 81%, plateau 82%. Mean SBP fell 16 mmHg from 148 (Punjab), about 15 mmHg from 144 (Maharashtra). Few patients reached steps 3+. Side effects not recorded; an unpublished sentinel survey found "about 12% of the individuals on amlodipine 10 mg had pedal edema". Authors flag regression to the mean. Kaur P et al., Global Heart 2024. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10959138/fullTextXML (PMC10959138, doi 10.5334/gh.1305) | published 2024-03-19 | OPENED | CITED
61	- D4-02-F18 | WHO 2021: monthly follow-up until target | Recommendation 7: "WHO suggests a monthly follow up after initiation or a change in antihypertensive medications until patients reach target." Conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence. Then every 3 to 6 months once controlled. Recommendation 8: nonphysician professionals may treat with training, prescribing authority, protocols and physician oversight. WHO Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults, 2021. https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/f062769d-f075-4a00-87af-0a2106e0bd04/content | published 2021 | OPENED | CITED
62	- D4-02-F19 | ISH 2020: control within 3 months, no step interval | ISH 2020 Figure 3: target a fall of at least 20/10 mmHg, ideally under 140/90 (essential), "Aim for BP control within 3 months". Table 9: once-daily drugs giving 24-hour control. Home BP for long-term follow-up of treated hypertension: "1-2 measurements per week or month"; diagnostic home schedule is morning and evening, two readings 1 min apart, over days or weeks. Monthly follow-up appears only for hypertensive emergencies. No interval between titration steps is stated. Unger T et al., Hypertension 2020;75:1334 onward (author copy, NWU repository). https://repository.nwu.ac.za/items/b6e36b1c-2c89-4af5-b12a-6d419a5b2e9c | published 2020-05 | OPENED | CITED
63	- D4-02-F20 | ESH 2023: monthly, but 2-weekly visits look better; no rigid rule | ESH 2023 follow-up section: "The initiation of drug therapy may be evaluated monthly until BP control is achieved. However, three large observational studies and one small RCT suggest that FU visits with shorter intervals (every 2 weeks) result in earlier and more common BP control rates." Then: visit frequency in titration "should not be subjected to rigid rules but differ according to BP phenotypes and response to treatment." Also: "A BP reduction is slower with monotherapy than with dual-drug combinations, with which a reduction in BP levels is expected within 1-2 weeks, although a further smaller progressive BP decline may continue for few more weeks." Once at target, visits every 3 to 6 months. Mancia G et al., J Hypertens 2023;41(12). https://journals.lww.com/jhypertension/fulltext/2023/12000/2023_esh_guidelines_for_the_management_of_arterial.2.aspx | published 2023-12 (online 2023-06) | OPENED | CITED
64	- D4-02-F21 | ESH 2023: long uncontrolled titration periods carry risk | ESH 2023 (section on time in control): data "emphasize the importance of avoiding a long titration period during which patients remain with an uncontrolled BP, particularly if their CV risk is high", one reason ESH starts most patients on two drugs. It also names physician inertia (failure to up-titrate) as a major cause of poor control; in ACCOMPLISH most of the 20% uncontrolled "had not been up-titrated". Same source as F20. https://journals.lww.com/jhypertension/fulltext/2023/12000/2023_esh_guidelines_for_the_management_of_arterial.2.aspx | published 2023-12 | OPENED | CITED
65	- D4-02-F22 | NICE NG136: no interval between steps; check doses and adherence first | NICE NG136 recommendations page has no titration interval in weeks or months. 1.4.15: "Use clinic blood pressure measurements to monitor the response to lifestyle changes or drug treatment". 1.4.44: before next-step treatment, check medicines are taken "at the optimal tolerated doses and discuss adherence". 1.4.19: home BP users need to know what to do if not at target; HBPM values are 5 mmHg lower than clinic. Diagnostic HBPM rule (1.2.7): 2 readings at least 1 minute apart, morning and evening, at least 4 days, ideally 7, discard day 1, average the rest. 1.4.50: after extra diuretic at step 4, check sodium, potassium and kidney function within 1 month. NICE NG136 (2019, amended 2023). https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations | recommendations 2019, amended 2023; page fetched 2026-11-14 | OPENED | CITED
66	- D4-02-F23 | ACC/AHA 2017 and AHA/ACC 2025: monthly until controlled (not opened) | Secondary sources say US guidance is follow-up at least monthly after starting or changing treatment until BP is controlled (2017 guideline wording recalled as "monthly intervals until control is achieved"; 2025 guideline published 14 Aug 2025 in Circulation, Hypertension and JACC replaces it). Guideline full text blocked (HTTP 403); wording not verified. https://www.pharmacist.com/Blogs/CEO-Blog/Article/bp-control-is-a-team-effort | 2025 | SNIPPET | SNIPPET
67	
68	### Q3. Trials that titrated faster
69	
70	- D4-02-F24 | Godwin 2010 cluster RCT: titrate every 2 weeks (Canada) | Cluster RCT, 19 family doctors, 156 patients not at target (Kingston, Ontario). Intervention: visit every 2 weeks for 16 weeks with regimen adjusted at each visit if not at target, versus usual care. At 12 months: office (BpTRU) systolic fell 14.7 vs 2.7 mmHg, diastolic 7.4 fall vs 0.6 rise; daytime ambulatory diastolic 4.5 vs 0.5 mmHg fall. 80% attended 4+ of 8 visits, 25% all 8; doctors raised drug number or dose at 52% of visits. Only 74% and 71% analysed. Side effects not reported in the abstract. Godwin M et al., Fam Pract 2010;27:55-61. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:19887462&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 19887462) | published online 2009-11-03; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
71	- D4-02-F25 | Turchin 2010 cohort: 2-week encounter intervals normalised BP fastest (US, diabetes) | Retrospective cohort, 5,042 hypertensive patients with diabetes, Boston primary care 2000 to 2005. Average encounter interval 1 month or less: BP normalised (under 130/85) after a median 1.5 months, falling 28.7 mmHg/month; interval over 1 month: 12.2 months at 2.6 mmHg/month. Interval 2 weeks or less vs 2 weeks to 1 month: median 0.7 vs 1.9 months to normal. Each extra month of interval: HR 0.764 for normalisation, adjusted for intensification rate. Observational, so sicker or keener patients may visit more. Turchin A et al., Hypertension 2010;56:68-74. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC3752696/fullTextXML (PMID 20497991) | published 2010-05-24; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
72	- D4-02-F26 | Sherman 2018 cohort: shorter intervals, more control (US, Kaiser) | Retrospective cohort, 95,957 newly diagnosed hypertensive patients, Kaiser Permanente Southern California, followed up to 1 year. Controlled group had more encounters (4.1 vs 3.1). As days between encounters rose from the 1 to under-14-day band upward, likelihood of control fell consistently; 180 days or more was worst. Observational. Sherman L et al., J Clin Hypertens 2018;20:429-37. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8031024/fullTextXML (PMID 29450983) | published 2018-02-16; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
73	- D4-02-F27 | Once controlled, 3 vs 6-monthly follow-up is equivalent | Randomised equivalence trial, 609 controlled patients, 50 Ontario practices, 3 years: 6-monthly follow-up equivalent to 3-monthly on mean BP, control, satisfaction and adherence; about 20% out of control at any time in both arms. Birtwhistle RV et al., BMJ 2004;328:204. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC318487/fullTextXML (PMID 14726370) | published 2004-01-15; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
74	- D4-02-F28 | TASMINH4: monthly home-BP-guided titration lowers BP with no excess adverse events (UK) | RCT, 142 UK practices, 1,182 patients over 35 with BP above 140/90. Patients self-measured twice morning and evening "for the first week of every month"; GPs titrated monthly from these readings. Home targets under 135/85 (under 80 years), 145/85 (80+), 135/75 (diabetes). At 12 months clinic systolic vs usual care: self-monitoring -3.5 mmHg (95% CI -5.8 to -1.2), telemonitoring -4.7 (-7.0 to -2.4). "Adverse events were similar between all three groups." Funded by NIHR and Omron UK. McManus RJ et al., Lancet 2018. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC5854463/fullTextXML (PMID 29499873) | published 2018-02-27 | OPENED | CITED
75	- D4-02-F29 | HyperLink: home telemonitoring plus pharmacist titration doubles control (US) | Cluster RCT, 16 Minnesota clinics, 450 uncontrolled adults, 12 months of intervention: pharmacists adjusted drugs from transmitted home readings. Control at both 6 and 12 months: 57.2% vs 30.0% usual care (P=.001); systolic fall greater by 10.7 mmHg at 6 months and 9.7 at 12 months; 71.8% vs 57.1% controlled at 18 months. The 2-week pharmacist contact interval during titration is our recollection only (full text not retrievable): NOT VERIFIED. Margolis KL et al., JAMA 2013. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:23821088&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 23821088) | published 2013-07-01; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
76	- D4-02-F30 | Fortnightly nurse titration clinic as effective as physician clinic (New Zealand) | Audit, 50 patients seen by a registrar then fortnightly clinical nurse specialist titration visits vs 50 in a physician clinic, Auckland 2010: same visits to discharge, same drugs at discharge (2.8), discharge BP 131/78 in the nurse group. Not randomised; no side-effect data in abstract. Taylor D et al., N Z Med J 2012. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:22722213&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 22722213) | published 2012-05-25; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
77	- D4-02-F31 | Pharmacist-led "expedited" telehealth titration: no falls or hypotension (US pilot) | Quality-improvement pilot, 42 patients with SBP 140+ on 2 or fewer drugs, home BP plus pharmacist telehealth with expedited titration to under 130/80: SBP 155.2 to 132.1, drugs 1.3 to 1.6, "no instances of falls or hypotension"; 31% reached under 130/80 on automated office BP. No control group. Ishak AM et al., J Clin Hypertens 2024. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:38192180&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 38192180) | published 2024-01-08; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
78	- D4-02-F32 | Amlodipine 5 to 10 mg: extra fall and oedema in Asian vs Western patients | Pooled post hoc analysis of Pfizer-run trials: patients on amlodipine 5 mg for 4 to 8 weeks, then titrated to 10 mg for another 4 to 8 weeks. Further fall from the 5 mg baseline: Asian (n=174; 40% Japan, rest China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Korea, Philippines, Taiwan, Thailand; no India) -13.3/-9.2 mmHg; Western (n=369) SBP -11.5. Peripheral oedema 6.3% Asian, 9.1% Western; none stopped for oedema in the Asian set. Uncontrolled (no placebo), so regression to the mean inflates the fall. Kario K, Robbins J, Jeffers BW. Vasc Health Risk Manag 2013;9:695. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC3821790/fullTextXML (PMC3821790) | published 2013 | OPENED | CITED
79	- D4-02-F33 | Nigeria primary-care protocol (losartan): 1-month steps | Nigeria Hypertension Treatment Protocol for Primary Health Care: step 1 amlodipine 5 mg; "After 1 month, measure BP again. If still high": step 2 amlodipine 5 + losartan 50; step 3 amlodipine 10 + losartan 100; step 4 add HCTZ 25 mg; then refer. Start at step 2 if BP 160/100 to under 180/110; at 180/110 or more give step 3 drugs and send to emergency within 1 hour. Telmisartan 40/80 "if available is preferable to losartan"; losartan barred in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age without contraception. https://resolvetosavelives.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/nigeria-hypertension-protocol-04-1.pdf | sheet undated (uploaded 2023-05; based on 2019 national protocol per search snippet) | OPENED | CITED
80	- D4-02-F34 | Nigeria triple-pill RCT: accelerated titration, more home control, no stops for adverse events | Open-label RCT, 300 Black African adults, Nigerian public clinics, 2022 to 2024. Low-dose telmisartan/amlodipine/indapamide pill (10/1.25/0.625, 20/2.5/1.25, 40/5/2.5 mg) "with accelerated up-titration" vs the Nigeria protocol (monthly steps from amlodipine 5 mg). Month 6 home systolic fall 31 vs 26 mmHg (difference -5.8, 95% CI -8.0 to -3.6); home control under 130/80 62% vs 28%; clinic control under 140/90 82% vs 72%. "No participants discontinued trial treatment due to adverse events." Exact titration interval: NOT FOUND (full text not retrievable). Ojji DB et al., JAMA 2024;332:1070-9. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:39215620&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 39215620) | published 2024-10-01; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
81	- D4-02-F35 | Amlodipine titrated every 2 weeks in an early trial: well tolerated | Double-blind placebo-controlled parallel trial, 30 patients with mild to moderate hypertension (Scotland): amlodipine 2.5 to 10 mg "titrated at 2 weekly intervals" over 8 weeks. Placebo-corrected fall at 8 weeks 16/12 mmHg supine, 14/4 standing; no heart-rate change; 2 patients had slight ankle oedema on 10 mg; BP back to baseline in a 4-week placebo washout. Trough plasma level rose in step with dose (2.5, 4.9, 10.5 ng/mL on 2.5, 5, 10 mg), so doubling the dose doubles the level. Small, old, sponsor role not stated in abstract. Webster J et al., Br J Clin Pharmacol 1987. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=PMCID:PMC1386394&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 2964253) | published 1987-12; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
82	
83	### Q4. Share of full effect at 1, 2 and 4 weeks
84	
85	- D4-02-F36 | Lasserson 2011: half the full effect in about 1 week, any class | Systematic review and nonlinear mixed-effects model, 18 trials, 4,168 drug-naive or washed-out patients started on one drug, office BP at least every 2 weeks for at least 4 weeks (searches to Dec 2009). Time to 50% of the estimated maximum fall: systolic 0.91 weeks (95% CI 0.74 to 1.10), diastolic 0.95 (0.75 to 1.15). Adding drug class did not improve the model, so the time course looked similar across classes. With a titration schedule the time to 50% was longer (systolic 1.2 vs 0.7 weeks; diastolic 1.4 vs 0.7) and the maximum larger. Authors: "Estimates of the maximum efficacy of antihypertensive agents can be made early after starting therapy." Office readings, not home. Lasserson DS, Buclin T, Glasziou P. Heart 2011;97:1771. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:21586424&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 21586424) | published online 2011-05-17; abstract only; full text blocked, HTTP 403 | OPENED | CITED
86	- D4-02-F37 | Implied share of full effect at 1, 2, 4 weeks | If the response follows a simple exponential approach to its maximum (the abstract says "asymptotic approach model"; the exact equation was not opened), fraction reached = 1 - 0.5^(t / t50). With t50 = 0.91 weeks: about 53% at 1 week, 78% at 2 weeks, 95% at 4 weeks. With t50 = 0.7 weeks (no titration): 63%, 86%, 98%. With t50 = 1.2 weeks (titration arms): 44%, 69%, 90%. OUR ARITHMETIC from F36; shape assumption unverified. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:21586424&format=json&resultType=core | 2011 | OPENED | OUR ARITHMETIC
87	- D4-02-F38 | Label time courses agree: most effect by 2 weeks, near full by 4 | Telmisartan: "Most of the antihypertensive effect is apparent within 2 weeks and maximal reduction is generally attained after 4 weeks" (F06). Olmesartan: onset within 1 week, "largely manifest after 2 weeks"; olmesartan plus HCTZ "near maximal at 4 weeks" (F12). Losartan: "substantially present within one week" but maximum in 3 to 6 weeks in some studies (F13). Lisinopril: optimal fall "may require two to four weeks" (F14). No US label for amlodipine or chlorthalidone gives a weeks-to-maximum figure. Labels as cited in F06, F12, F13, F14. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=20a60231-64f0-4751-aa81-6c0e64334179 | labels 2023 to 2026 | OPENED | CITED
88	
89	### Q5. Does the response keep growing after 4 weeks (chlorthalidone, telmisartan)
90	
91	- D4-02-F39 | Thiazide mechanism changes over weeks: volume first, then resistance | 11 hypertensive patients on HCTZ 50 mg twice daily (high dose, 1970s). At 48 hours: BP, cardiac output, plasma volume and extracellular fluid all down, while total peripheral resistance rose (a reflex). At 6 and 8 weeks: BP and volumes still down, but peripheral resistance had fallen and cardiac output returned to baseline. So the early fall is from salt and water loss and the later, lasting fall is from lower vessel resistance ("reverse autoregulation"). Small, old, Western study. Shah S, Khatri I, Freis ED. Am Heart J 1978. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:637001&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 637001) | published 1978-05; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
92	- D4-02-F40 | Chlorthalidone mechanism: sodium, renin rise, lower noradrenaline sensitivity | 23 untreated hypertensive patients, chlorthalidone 100 mg/day (well above today's doses) for 6 weeks: BP and exchangeable body sodium fell; blood volume and heart rate unchanged; plasma renin rose markedly; pressor response to noradrenaline fell. Our gloss, not in the abstract: rising renin is the body's counter-regulation, which an added ARB blocks. Weidmann P et al., Kidney Int 1983. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:6341684&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 6341684) | published 1983-02; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
93	- D4-02-F41 | Chlorthalidone works mostly by week 2 (office BP) | Randomised single-blind crossover, untreated hypertensive patients (US), chlorthalidone 12.5 mg force-titrated to 25 mg vs HCTZ 25 force-titrated to 50 mg, office BP every 2 weeks, ABPM at baseline and week 8. Week 2 office systolic fall: chlorthalidone 12.5 mg -15.7 mmHg vs HCTZ 25 mg -4.5 (P=0.001). Week 8 (after forced titration): -17.1 vs -10.8 (not significant). Week 8 24-h ambulatory systolic: -12.4 vs -7.4 (P=0.054); night -13.5 vs -6.4 (P=0.009). Only 30 completed period 1. So most of chlorthalidone's office effect showed at 2 weeks; HCTZ caught up more slowly. Ernst ME et al., Hypertension 2006. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:16432050&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 16432050) | published 2006-01-23; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
94	- D4-02-F42 | India: chlorthalidone 6.25 mg lowers 24-h BP at 4 and 12 weeks; HCTZ 12.5 mg does not | Double-blind RCT, 54 stage 1 patients in India (CTRI/2013/07/003793), 12 weeks: chlorthalidone 6.25 mg (n=16), HCTZ 12.5 mg (n=18), HCTZ controlled-release 12.5 mg (n=20). ABPM at 0, 4, 12 weeks. All three lowered office BP at weeks 4 and 12. Only chlorthalidone (and HCTZ-CR) lowered 24-h and night ambulatory BP, already at week 4. HCTZ 12.5 mg "merely converted sustained hypertension into masked hypertension" because it wears off within the day. Small trial; industry-linked authors (not checked). Pareek AK et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2016. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:26821625&format=json&resultType=core (PMID 26821625) | published 2016-02-01; abstract only | OPENED | CITED
95	- D4-02-F43 | Telmisartan, EU-style SmPC: maximum at 4 to 8 weeks, a caution before raising the dose | Swedish telmisartan generic (Elicator) SmPC, section 4.2: "When considering raising the dose, it must be borne in mind that the maximum antihypertensive effect is generally attained four to eight weeks after the start of treatment". Section 5.1: activity "gradually becomes evident within 3 hours"; maximum "4 to 8 weeks after the start of treatment"; 80 mg almost completely blocks the angiotensin II pressor response, still measurable at 48 h; on stopping, BP returns over several days without rebound. Section 5.2: half-life over 20 hours and "no evidence of clinically relevant accumulation" at the recommended dose. DISAGREEMENT: US label says maximal "by about 4 weeks" and accumulation index 1.5 to 2.0 (F05, F06). SmPC revised 2012-11-29. https://docetp.mpa.se/LMF/Elicator%20tablet%20ENG%20SmPC_09001bee807af83e.pdf | SmPC revision 2012-11-29 | OPENED | CITED
96	- D4-02-F44 | India: chlorthalidone's ambulatory effect nearly doubled from week 4 to week 12 | Same Indian trial as F42, as reported by Healio: chlorthalidone 6.25 mg lowered 24-h ambulatory systolic BP by 6.74 mmHg at 4 weeks and 12.11 mmHg at 12 weeks. So about 56% of the 12-week ambulatory effect was present at 4 weeks (OUR ARITHMETIC: 6.74 / 12.11 = 0.557). Only 16 patients on chlorthalidone; at a very low dose (6.25 mg). Contrast: Thalitone label office data (F10) show little growth after week 2 to 4; Ernst 2006 office data (F41) show most of the effect at week 2. Healio news report of Pareek 2016. https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/20160308/lowdose-chlorthalidone-superior-to-lowdose-hydrochlorothiazide-for-sustained-bp-lowering | article dated 2016-01-27; secondary news report | OPENED | CITED
97	
98	## NOT FOUND / NOT SEARCHED
99	
100	- NOT FOUND: a label, SmPC or study stating weeks to maximal BP effect for amlodipine, or a time-course study after an amlodipine 5 to 10 mg step. Only steady state (F01), the label titration interval (F03) and fixed-endpoint trials (F32, F35).
101	- NOT FOUND: a trial randomising 2-week against 4-week titration intervals with side effects (hypotension, falls, creatinine, potassium) as outcomes. Godwin (F24) compared 2-weekly visits with usual care; the rest is observational (F25, F26) or uncontrolled (F31).
102	- NOT FOUND: the titration interval in the Nigeria triple-pill trial (F34). JAMA full text could not be retrieved.
103	- NOT FOUND (not verified): exact ACC/AHA 2017 and AHA/ACC 2025 wording on follow-up interval. Journal pages returned HTTP 403 (F23 is SNIPPET).
104	- NOT FOUND: the 2-week pharmacist contact interval in HyperLink (F29). Recollection only, not confirmed.
105	- NOT FOUND: South Asian time-course data beyond the IHCI programme (F17) and the small Pareek trial (F42, F44). Lasserson (F36), Ernst (F41), Shah (F39), Godwin (F24) and Turchin (F25) are Western data only. The Asian amlodipine pool (F32) has no Indian patients.
106	- NOT FOUND: the model equation in Lasserson 2011; full text blocked (HTTP 403). F37 assumes an exponential approach.
107	- NOT SEARCHED: Gujarat HEARTS sheet text. The Punjab and Madhya Pradesh IHCI sheets (F15, F16) were used as the nearest Indian versions.
108	- NOT SEARCHED: Indian (CDSCO) label or package-insert wording on time to effect.
109	- NOT SEARCHED: telmisartan trials with BP measured beyond 8 weeks; HCTZ 25 to 50 mg time course; losartan 50 to 100 mg time course.
110	- NOT SEARCHED: the WHO 2021 evidence profile behind recommendation 7 (monthly follow-up).
111	- NOT SEARCHED: the EMA Micardis SmPC itself (ema.europa.eu returned HTTP 429). A Swedish generic SmPC (F43) was used instead.
112

1	# D4 brief: the biology deep dive (Round 4, 14 Nov 2026, about 00:40 AM India time)
2	
3	Read this whole file, then read `D0-brief.md` sections 3 to 6 and 8 in this folder. D0's fact rule, schemas, note layout and style apply in full. Where this file adds to D0, this file wins.
4	
5	## Why this round
6	
7	The team's document is built on trial abstracts and policy papers. It has little of the physiology underneath: why one patient responds to a drug and another does not, how fast a dose change works, how much blood pressure moves on its own, why each safety check exists, which lab values matter and how fast they move, and how to tell from the body (not from the patient's word) whether the medicine was taken. That layer is what would make the product hard to copy. The reader of your note is the team's biology student, who will turn it into protocol rules and product features.
8	
9	## The product it serves
10	
11	A home blood-pressure step loop for India. A patient sends home cuff readings. Software runs the state's published step protocol (Gujarat HEARTS sheet) from a data file and drafts a dose change; a doctor approves it with one tap. Before any step-up it asks whether the medicine was taken. The protocol: step 1 amlodipine 5 mg; step 2 amlodipine 10 mg ("after 30 days measure BP again, if still high"); step 3 add telmisartan 40 mg; step 4 telmisartan 80 mg (requires blood sugar, urea, creatinine, urine protein; abnormal means refer; if no specialist, withdraw telmisartan and add chlorthalidone); step 5 add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if unavailable). Telmisartan and chlorthalidone are barred in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age without effective contraception. A Nigeria protocol uses losartan. The loop uses home readings: two readings 1 minute apart, morning and evening, on days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle; at least 3 valid days, aiming for 7; "still high" is a home mean of 135/85 or more; 180/110 or more triggers urgent review.
